mcqs.question: According to P_dynamic = C x V^2 x f, if you double the clock frequency and keep everything else constant, what happens to dynamic power?
mcqs.explanation: Frequency appears linearly in the formula, so doubling f doubles dynamic power directly, unlike voltage which appears squared. Confusing the linear frequency term with the quadratic voltage term is the most common error here.

mcqs.question: Why has static (leakage) power grown from negligible to a significant fraction of total chip power over successive process generations?
options: Because clock frequencies have decreased over time
Because as transistors shrink, leakage current through nominally-off transistors doesn't shrink proportionally, so it becomes a larger share of the power budget
Because modern chips no longer use dynamic power at all
Because static power only exists in chips manufactured after a certain year
mcqs.explanation: Leakage is a physical side effect of transistor scaling — smaller transistors leak more relative to their size, so as chips have shrunk, static power's share has grown even while total chip area and dynamic switching activity change too. Clock frequencies have generally increased, not decreased, and dynamic power is still very much present in modern chips.

mcqs.question: Chip A draws more instantaneous power than Chip B but finishes a task in half the time. Which statement could be true?
options: Chip A always uses more total energy since it draws more power
Chip A could use less total energy than Chip B, since energy is power integrated over time and A finishes much faster
Power and energy are always identical for the same task
Energy only depends on peak power, not on how long a task runs
mcqs.explanation: Energy = power integrated over time, so a higher-power-but-shorter-duration chip can easily use less total energy than a lower-power-but-longer-duration one. Power and energy are related but not identical quantities, and duration is exactly what the naive "higher power = worse" comparison misses.

mcqs.question: Why is reducing voltage generally the most effective single lever for cutting a chip's dynamic power?
options: Because voltage has no effect on transistor switching speed
Because dynamic power scales with voltage squared, so a given percentage cut in voltage reduces power by a much larger percentage than the same cut in frequency
Because reducing voltage always improves performance as a side effect
Because voltage is the only term in the dynamic power equation
mcqs.explanation: The quadratic voltage term means a modest voltage reduction yields an outsized power saving compared to cutting frequency (which only scales linearly) — the core reason DVFS targets voltage first. Voltage very much affects switching speed (which is the real constraint on how low it can go), reducing it costs performance rather than improving it, and it's one of three terms in the formula, not the only one.
